column2: At its root it measures ten thousand, and it has expanded to the same extent; in length it is the same number of yojanas, risen like a pillar of the three worlds,
lighting the earth and sky with its golden and jewelled peaks — where the sun's charioteer's son (Kashyapa's son, Aruna) goes and becomes rayless, his splendour lost.
With a golden-bodied form, gold-bright, she arrived at Mandara, which itself dims the sun's splendour by its radiance;
making herself, for the king's desires and aims, seated on a rock, divine, of blue lustre, seven yojanas broad.
On that rock, O king, stands a linga of the thunderbolt-bearer (Indra), ten cubits across and higher in number;
it is called the Vrishalinga, supreme, like a palace and cloud. There, O best of Brahmins, the girl made excellent music,
joined with strings and rhythm, destroying fatigue. Near that linga, becoming the lady,
with melody and rhythm joined with the Gandhara note — while the song, increasing love, was proceeding, O king,
there arose a longing even in the immovable beings, O lords of sages; there had never been such a song, divine or not.
The song sung from Mohini's mouth was a song that bewilders beings.
Hearing the song, the Naked One (Shiva) himself, in that very form, desiring to enjoy the fair-limbed woman, tormented by love, moved, ashamed before Parvati's sight, toward that Mohini.

I was appointed by my father for your protection and welfare. I, desiring dharma, must in all ways do my father's word.
naradapuran:133:30	For a son there is no other dharma than his father's word. With me holding the staff as ruler, Yama is never your ruler.
naradapuran:133:31	Knowing thus, you should remember the Garuda-bannered Lord; Janardana is to be worshipped by offering to Brahman,
naradapuran:133:32	giving up possessiveness and by what is prescribed for one's own class; by which your worlds will be imperishable, without doubt.
naradapuran:133:33	This path, higher than the ancestors' path, is shown to you, O people; be engaged in rites offered to Brahman and be knowers of knowledge.
naradapuran:133:34	One must not eat on Hari's day. The path of ancestors is eternal. A special thing is told by me to you: abiding in Brahman,
naradapuran:133:35	to be practised by the knowers of truth; return is hard to come by. That one must fast on Hari's day is a fixed rule.
Having persuaded all the people and reassured them again and again, the sick (or the one on whom dharma lies) neither by day nor by night sleeps.
He wanders everywhere in valour, making the earth free of thorns; the drum resounds always, on the head of the enemy of the deer (lion).
People without eating on Dvadashi, free of possessiveness, and in the three kinds of duties, the Lord Hari should be contemplated.
The god who carries offerings to gods and ancestors is that very Supreme Person; he who in the sun, in space, in emission, is the Lord of the world
is to be remembered by all men desiring dharma, desire and wealth. So too in the path of the good prescribed by one's own class, it is Madhava;
he alone is the enjoyer and to be enjoyed; he alone is the Supreme Person. His application fits all rites.
So they cry, O Brahmins, with a drum like a cloud's roar. Having thus learned dharma, then Dharmangada's father,
knowing his son endowed with rites and greater than himself, O Brahmins, joyfully said to his wife, who stood like another Lakshmi:

Sandhyavali, I am blessed, and you too, fair-hued one: a son moon-white on earth was born of us both.
naradapuran:133:45	Liberation is heard of with the ears; none anywhere has seen it. That liberation, born of a good son, has been gained by us in greater measure.
naradapuran:133:46	When a son is endowed with modesty, conduct and valour, mighty, fair-hipped one, the father's liberation in the house is certain.
naradapuran:133:47	Bliss is Brahma's form; the father by a son becomes of a hundred blisses, by good and auspicious deeds.
naradapuran:133:48	Nothing in the moving and unmoving world, goddess, is equal to this: a good son takes up the burden from his father and bears it.
naradapuran:133:49	I, delighted, shall go to the forest to play and to hunt deer, wandering at will, O large-eyed one, and freed from sin to protect the people.
Vamadeva said to him: "Say; what shall I give you? Nothing is ungiveable, O king, to you who have come to my house now.
He who gives on earth what is desired by a king, O protector of the earth, a drum on Vishnu's day forbidding the people to eat..."
Then the king said to the Brahmin, with folded hands: "I have obtained everything by seeing your pair of feet.
I have one doubt for a long time, Brahmin. I ask you, the best of Brahmins, breaker of all doubts:
by what good deed is my wife the beauty of the three worlds, who always looks on me with eyes more full of love than Cupid?
Wherever the lovely goddess places her foot, there the earth reveals treasures.
Her body is free of old age, free of wrinkles and grey hair, O best of sages; it always shines like the autumn moon.
Without fire she prepares the six tastes; the little food she cooks, ten millions eat from it.
Devoted to her husband, charitable, bringing happiness to all beings; even in sleep she is not disrespected by a word.
The son born of her has always stayed under my command; I alone, O best of Brahmins, am the one blessed in sons on earth.
A son devoted to his father, greater in a heap of virtues; I am known on earth as lord of one continent;
my son is greater, protector of the seven continents, by whom a king's daughter was brought for me, O best of Brahmins,
named Vidyullekha, after conquering kings in battle. Then that lord, rich in beauty and wealth,
in six months having conquered in battle and disarmed all, went to the kingdom of women, conquering those women in battle,
took from among them eight fair-limbed women, and gave them all to me, bowing again and again.
Whatever divine garments and whatever jewels there are on earth, my son gave them to me, as described by his mother.
He crosses the entire earth, many yojanas, in a day, and returns at night to anoint my feet.
At midnight he massages my limbs and stands armoured at the door, awakening servants whose senses are weighed down by sleep.
So my body, O best of sages, is free of disease. My happiness is immeasurable; my beloved is under my control at home.
Horses, elephants, endless wealth and grain: all the people on earth obey my command.
By the power of what deed is this happiness mine now? Whether done in this birth or in a former one,
tell me, Brahmin, my merit, reflecting by your own wisdom."
No disease in the body, a beloved under control at home, prosperity, devotion to Nrihari, honour for the learned, ability to give to Brahmins — I think these arise from merit.

One who does his father's word with mind, speech and body: for him bathing in the Ganga happens every day.
naradapuran:135:23	One who disregards his father's word and goes to bathe in the heavenly river — that son has no purity; so says the Vedic tradition.
naradapuran:135:24	Go as you wish, O king; your task is done. By Hari's grace a son, a doer of merit, has been born in your line.
Thus addressed by the sage, he mounted his horse and went swiftly, glorious, like the wind itself.
Seeing all the mountains, forests and rivers, all the wonders, lakes and groves, the king
soon reached Mount Mandara, after circling the White Mountain and Gandhamadana.
Having crossed great Meru and seen the Uttara Kurus, shining with the lustre of a hundred suns, covered all around with gold,
rubbed by Hari's arms, flowing with gold juice, the region thick with mountains, adorned with many minerals,
with many streams and many caves, filled with tens of thousands of rivers, washed with the holy waters of the Ganga,
with trusting groups of young women, attending their loved ones' delight, with ripe, fragrant fruits, pot-sized, O king,
adorned with fruits like the breasts of young women, filled with the humming of bees and sounding with the cuckoo's note,
the mountain resounding on all sides with the cries of many creatures — seeing it, the king entered the great mountain.
Wishing to climb out of curiosity, searching for a path to ascend, he looked all around where the whole throng of trees and birds
was moving, seized by the sound arisen from Mohini's mouth, rushing along; the king went swiftly with that same sound.
That sound, arisen from Mohini's mouth, entered his ear too; bewildered by it, leaving his horse as if stepping over three strides,
the king in a moment suddenly saw the mountain-path charmed by Mohini's song. Standing on the mountain, bright as heated gold, as if the staff of Love made,
as if worshipping Shakra's linga in the sky for the world's good, like the embodiment of the earth's patience, like a heap of beauty of the mountain's daughter,
like the coast of the ocean endowed with beauty, her body called the house of Rati, pulling suddenly the three-eyed (Shiva) at the linga for the gods' amusement —
the desire in the mind of that doer of merit, seeing Mohini's form, he stood bewildered; the king fell, pierced by the arrow of love for Mohini.
His body seized by a violent fever, he crept quickly near her; the fair-eyed one looked at the creeping king with a sidelong glance.
Letting go of the lute, she stopped her song and suddenly considered the act sinful; shaking off flocks of beasts and birds with her fine garment, stopping her cheek and arm,
the goddess, sweet with fragrant breath, went to the king's side, leaving Hara, the most worshipped, the good linga, and standing beside him, of generous ways.
Mohini, with eyes like stainless lotus petals, spoke a sweet, charming word to Rukmangada, tormented by love's arrows: "Rise, O king; I am under your control.
Why do you waste this body with swooning, you who bear this great burden of the earth? O king, you would carry it as a straw, seeing this my captivating form.
Why are you bewildered like a weak cow sunk in mud? You are steady; why do you mock yourself, you of noble deeds?
If you have a wish, O lord of kings, in a charming union favourable to me, give a gift stated by good dharma and enjoy me, who knows love, as your own maidservant."

Whatever merit I have done since birth, fair one, all of it is yours, fair-thighed, if I do not do your word.
naradapuran:136:19	In the meantime this dharma has been given to me: become my wife, O fair-bodied one. Through your beauty an agitation has suddenly come upon me.
naradapuran:136:20	I am the son of Ritadhvaja, the king named Rukmangada, born in Ikshvaku's line; my son is Dharmangada.
naradapuran:136:21	O lovely-eyed one, I entered a thicket on a pretext of hunting; there I saw a charming hermitage of Vamadeva in the forest.
naradapuran:136:22	Having talked with the sage there, I was dismissed; mounting my excellent horse I came to see Mandara.
naradapuran:136:23	Wandering the best of mountains, curious in mind, the song that came from your mouth reached my ear.
naradapuran:136:24	Drawn by that song, I came near you. You, lovely-eyed, came within the path of my sight.
naradapuran:136:25	Then I fainted, goddess, and fell senseless on the ground. Now I have my senses by the nectar of your words.
naradapuran:136:26	I feel as if born again, O bewilderer of the world. By giving an answer you should show favour.
Thus asked by the king, Mohini gave a reply: "I, born of Brahma, have come for your sake, O king,
having heard your fame and been touched by love, leaving Mandara, the golden mountain, and all the gods led by Vishvambhara,
here I stay intent on austerity with concentrated mind, worshipping the God of gods, Shankara, with the gift of song.
I think the gift of song is very dear to the gods, greater than all gifts, O king, giving an endless goal,
by which the Lord of beings is pleased and at once repays. I have obtained you, whom I desired, protector of the earth.
You are pleased with me, O king; I am pleased with you."
Having so spoken, Mohini, with a face like the king of Brahmins (the moon), took the king's hand with speed and raised him from lying on the ground, like Indra's staff.

A wife should stay in her husband's place, even if it lacks prosperity. That golden Meru is said to be near.
naradapuran:137:18	Meru is called Manoratha, where you, Lord, delight, leaving your husband's place or your own father's.
naradapuran:137:19	A woman devoted to dwelling in her father's place sinks into darkness; even without all dharma, a woman becomes a sow.
naradapuran:137:20	Knowing this fault, how shall I stay on Mandara? I shall go with you, you being my Lord in happiness and sorrow.
Hearing Mohini's words, the king, glad of heart, embraced the fair-thighed one and said this:

You will be above all my wives. Do not fear, fair-thighed one, by which sorrow would arise.
naradapuran:137:23	You will be dearer than my life in my house, fair-browed one. Come, let us go, slender-limbed, to the city for happiness.
naradapuran:137:24	Enjoy pleasures with me there, dear, as you wish.
Thus addressed, she, with a face bright as the moon, set out with Rukmangada, anklets sounding, dragging the splendour of the mountain's daughter, for the destruction of herself.
From that day he had consumption; the husband wasted day by day. Worms arose in his secret parts from wounds and bad sores.
After a few days, as the sun was seen like a lamp, the husband, his splendour destroyed and senses agitated, said to me,
crying day and night: "I am your servant, O lovely one. Save me, who have come for refuge; I shall not go to another's woman."
Hearing his crying, frightened, O king, I told her everything: "How may my husband be happy?"
She also gave a medicine, a second one for quieting the burning; when the medicine was given, the husband was at once healthy.
The burning born of the earlier powder was quenched by that medicine. From then on my husband was under my control, obedient to my word.
In time I died and went to the tortures of hell. I was burned in a copper frying-pan for fifteen ages.
Made into fine pieces the size of sesame seeds, many times, with a small remainder of sin, I was brought down to earth.
A house-lizard's form was made for me by the son of the Sun (Yama). So I have stayed here, O king, ten thousand years.
Any young woman, O king, who practises controlling her husband in vain, of bad conduct, is burned in the copper pan.
The husband is lord, the goal, the husband the god and the teacher; how can she who controls him obtain happiness?
She goes to a hundred animal wombs with worms and leprosy; therefore, O king, women should always do what the husband says.
I shall go again to a wretched womb, full of sin, if you do not uplift me today, who have come for refuge,
by giving me the merit born of Vijaya: the Shravana-Dvadashi which you kept at the confluence, holy,
that destroys sin in the Sarayu and Ganga, sends ghosts away, holy, granting the mind's desires —
in the house of one who, even at home, remembers Hari, O king, it gives the fruit of attaining all holy places, without doubt.
What is given, chanted, offered, and done in worship of the gods and the like on Vijaya day, O king, is all imperishable.
Give me such merit as is the fruit of that fast — fasting on Dvadashi and breaking the fast on the thirteenth,
the fruit of twelve years of fasting, obtained by one fast. Show mercy, O king; you are dharma embodied on earth,
destroyer of the path of Yama, save me, in great distress." Hearing the house-lizard's words, Mohini said:

Each person eats his own deed, consisting of pleasure and pain, Lord. So what use is this sinful one, wicked to her husband,
naradapuran:138:51	who brought her husband under control by protective powders and the like, O king? What is done for the good brings fame and heaven.
naradapuran:138:52	What is done from sin brings ruin to both; milk mixed with sugar given to a snake only increases poison; so is what is done from sin.
naradapuran:138:53	Abandon this sinner; let us go to the city. For those attached to the business of birth, one's own happiness is destroyed.
Rukmangada said: "O daughter of Brahma, how can you say such a word? This is not the conduct of the good, fair-faced one.
Sinners are those who seek their own happiness and torment others; the good are for the benefit of others, fair-thighed one.
The moon, sun, cloud, earth, fire, water, sandal, trees and the good exist for others' benefit.
It is heard that there was a king Harishchandra, fair-faced one, who lived in an outcaste's house, selling his wife and son,
afraid of untruth, going from sorrow to greater sorrow. The gods led by Shakra, pleased with his truth, offered the king Harishchandra a boon.
He, true to his word, said to the gods led by Brahma: "If the gods are pleased, you should give me a boon:
let all this city with its trees, reptiles, children, old and young, women and animals,
though sinful, go to the heavenly state. I shall take Ayodhya's sin and go surely to hell.
Leaving the people on earth, I will not go alone to heaven, O tigers among the wise; this is true as I have said."
Knowing his steadiness, the city went with him to heaven with the leave of Indra and the others.
He too stayed in heaven, the king with his city, honoured even by the immortals, in a vehicle going at will.
Out of compassion, goddess, Dadhichi gave his bones for the gods' benefit, hearing that the gods were defeated by the demons;
King Shibi long ago gave his own flesh for the pigeon to a hungry hawk, O fair-limbed.
There was a king, Jimutavahana, on earth long ago, and he too gave his life to a serpent, O fair-faced one.
Therefore, goddess, a king should be merciful; the cloud rains equally on pure and impure alike.
The moon pleases outcastes and fallen with his rays. Therefore I shall uplift this suffering house-lizard,
by my own merit as Nahusha did by his grandsons." Setting aside Mohini, he said to the house-lizard:
I have given, I have given you the merit born of Vijaya. Go to Vishnu's worlds, freed of all stain.
By his word, suddenly, O king, adorned with divine ornaments, leaving that old body born of a house-lizard,
she took leave of the king and went, lighting the ten directions, as if parting the sky with a path to the wonderful Vaishnava abode.
